sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Bernalillo County
sections.html:
Two elected offices split the work. The Assessor values property and prepares the tax roll. The Treasurer bills and collects. Both are at Alvarado Square, 415 Silver Ave SW in Albuquerque, the county seat. The Assessor's number is (505) 222-3700 and the Treasurer's is (505) 468-7031.

Bernalillo County is New Mexico's most populous, with more than 676,000 residents, about 106,000 of them outside city limits in Albuquerque, Los Ranchos and Tijeras. Because parcels range from city lots to unincorporated land, the tax rate depends on the taxing districts around a given address.

The Assessor's job covers real property, business personal property, livestock and manufactured homes. It notifies owners of value and hands the finished roll to the Treasurer.

Value is fixed on January 1, notices go out by April 1, rates are set in September, the roll goes to the Treasurer by October 1, and bills are mailed by early November.

EventTimingOffice
Property valued as of its conditionJanuary 1Assessor
Exemption and Head of Family applicationsLast day of February, or 30 days after the Notice of ValueAssessor
Notices of Value mailedBy April 1Assessor
Valuation certified to the stateJune 15Assessor
Delinquent notices mailedAbout June 10Treasurer
Rates setSeptemberState Dept. of Finance and Administration
Tax roll deliveredOctober 1Assessor to Treasurer
Bills mailed, first half dueNovember 1 and November 10Treasurer
Second half dueApril 10Treasurer

When November 1 falls on a weekend, the Treasurer mails bills the next business day. Owners not on the 10-month payment agreement can pay in full or in two installments.

Taxable value is one-third of assessed value. Exemptions come off that figure, and then the mill rate is applied. Net taxable value means taxable value minus exemptions such as Head of Family and the veteran exemption.

The state sets mill rates, and they differ by taxing district. The Treasurer posts rate charts for 2016 to 2025, and the Assessor's property search shows the figures for one address. In the latest cycle many rates fell, but rising valuations, a new taxing district and added tax initiatives still pushed bills up across the county.

New Mexico caps yearly growth in the taxable value of residential property at 3%. The cap limits assessment growth and does not limit the mill rate.

The Assessor offers Head of Family, veteran and disabled veteran exemptions, plus a value freeze. None of them needs a separate protest form.

  • Head of Family takes $2,000 off taxable value for one property per household in the state.
  • The veteran exemption takes up to $10,000 off taxable value with a certificate from the state's veteran service commission. Once granted, it stays on the record.
  • Disabled veterans can exempt a percentage of the primary residence based on their VA disability rating.
  • The value freeze is for owners 65 or older with modified gross income of $42,900 or less, or disabled owners at $41,900 or less. It stops assessed value from rising 3% and does not freeze the tax rate.

Apply within 30 days after the Notice of Value is mailed. The Assessor's tax savings page has the forms. A value freeze never forces you to sell at the frozen value.

File a protest with the Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing, online through the appeal portal or at 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal meeting with a field appraiser follows. If the value is still not settled, the Protest Valuation Review Board holds a hearing. An owner who gets an amended Notice of Value has 30 days from the amended mailing date.

Business personal property, manufactured home and livestock protests run on a separate spring window, so check the Assessor's protest page each year.

If you miss the window, you can still pay the bill and file a claim for refund in the Second Judicial District Court at 400 Lomas Blvd NW. The Treasurer says the claim is due by the 60th day after the first installment due date, and the bill must be paid first. The Assessor lists a $132 court filing fee. Call the court self-help center at 505-841-6702 to confirm the cutoff before you rely on it.

If a protest is still pending in December, the Treasurer recommends paying the first half on the original bill. A new bill and a refund follow if the protest succeeds, and paying avoids late fees if it does not.

Late charges are interest of 1% per month plus a penalty of 1% per month, with the penalty capped at 5% and a minimum of $5. They start December 10 for the first half and May 10 for the second.

You can pay in person on the first floor of 415 Silver Ave SW, online through the county's payment vendor, or by mail to PO Box 27800, Albuquerque, NM 87125-7800. The Treasurer warns against bank bill-pay services because of mailing delays, misrouting and no confirmation. Owners are liable even if a bill never arrives. About 10,600 bills came back undelivered in the 2025 cycle, mostly for outdated addresses, so keep your mailing address current.

Delinquent notices go out around June 10.

The owner of record on January 1 is liable for that year's tax. A manufactured home needs a tax release before it can be sold, moved or traded. Title companies pull the balance and pay it from the sale proceeds.

A manufactured home owner gets the tax release from the Treasurer, showing current and prior years paid, and starts the process at the Assessor with proof of ownership. Land and a manufactured home on it get separate notices and bills unless the home has been converted to real property. Public improvement district charges transfer to the buyer, and a seller can prepay the balance.

After closing, file the residential transfer affidavit with the Assessor within 30 days, as covered in our Bernalillo County Clerk guide. Sellers with back taxes, an inherited house or a tenant in place often sell as-is for cash to skip repairs and showings. The tax balance comes out of the proceeds either way.

Before you list, ask the Treasurer for the current balance, ask the Assessor to confirm your exemptions are on the record, and tell the title company if you have a protest pending.

faqs.q: When are Bernalillo County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 10 and the second half April 10. Late fees begin December 10 and May 10.

faqs.q: Who sets property values in Bernalillo County?
faqs.a: The elected County Assessor sets values and mails Notices of Value by April 1. The elected Treasurer bills and collects the tax, and the state sets mill rates each September.

faqs.q: How do I protest my Bernalillo County valuation?
faqs.a: File a protest form with the Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing, online or at 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal meeting and, if needed, a Protest Valuation Review Board hearing follow.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Bernalillo County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company normally pays the balance, including penalty and interest, from the sale proceeds at closing. Confirm the figure with the Treasurer at (505) 468-7031.

faqs.q: Does Bernalillo County send a bill if a mortgage company pays my taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Every owner receives a bill even when a lender pays. The bill lists the mortgage company that requested the amount, and the owner stays responsible for making sure it is paid.
